abstract_quote: Based on data gathered through CrowdTangle and Twitter API, we selected the 250 most shared/retweeted posts for each dataset (n=500) and examined if they contained disinformation, who posted it, and what strategy was used to legitimize this discourse.
note: Clean disclosure of the top-250 cut per platform; Methods repeat it ('we selected the 250 most retweeted tweets and the 250 most shared Facebook posts to analyze'). The abstract reports no percentage; the 70% (Twitter) and 51% (Facebook) disinformation shares are in the body only.

abstract_quote: A dataset of 47,567 posts from 29 channels was collected and analyzed using a mixed-methods design integrating natural language processing, social network analysis of co-posting ties, and rhetorical analysis. ... Disinformation was less prevalent than propaganda
note: NOT_CURATED?: the 0.54% is over ALL posts of 29 purposively chosen channels; the curation is at channel level only and there is no rank cut on posts (cf. the September flag on 2-s2.0-105008921175). Methods: 'I collected all posts shared by a selection of 29 highly popular channels from the three mentioned types' (channel details in Appendix 1). The abstract gives n but not how the channels were picked, and no percentage, only 'Disinformation was less prevalent than propaganda'.

abstract_quote: We validate our methodology on a case study on the 2017 French presidential election (60 million Twitter exchanges between more than 2.4 million users)
note: NOT_CURATED?: Politoscope is a continuous keyword/actor-tracked collection ('almost 60 million tweets concerning more than three thousands of the key French political figures and few dozens political keywords', Data section), not a top-N or hand-picked item set. The abstract names the election and the size but not the tracking rule. The 0.0081% Decodex fake-news share is not in the abstract (only 'a differential echo chamber effect').

abstract_quote: Here, we use a dataset of 171 million tweets in the five months preceding the election day to identify 30 million tweets, from 2.2 million users, which contain a link to news outlets. Based on a classification of news outlets curated by www.opensources.co, we find that 25% of these tweets spread either fake or extremely biased news.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the 30.7M denominator is every tweet linking to a classified news outlet within a keyword collection (171M tweets mentioning Clinton or Trump, per the frozen row), i.e. a full topical keyword sample with no rank cut. The abstract describes the news-link filter but not the Clinton/Trump keyword query. The headline 25% pools fake and extremely biased news.

abstract_quote: In this work, we analyze information dissemination within WhatsApp, focusing on publicly accessible political-oriented groups, collecting all shared messages during major social events in Brazil ... We then deepen our analysis by identifying the presence of misinformation among the shared images using labels provided by journalists and by a proposed automatic procedure based on Google searches.
note: The abstract says 'collecting all shared messages' and mentions journalist labels, but never that the fact-checked set was the 61 most-shared election-campaign images (Section 5.1: 'We created a list of the most shared images during the election campaign period and gave them to one of the most important fact-checking agencies in Brazil, Lupa'; 47 of 61 were factual). It gives no n and no percentage, and reads as if the labels cover the shared images in general.

abstract_quote: By analyzing information-sharing behavior on 252 Facebook pages, our study highlights the wide variety of information sources shared by several political communities, notably news published by partisan websites or activist blogs.
note: Abstract gives n=252 only. Methods: after 75 interviews with party supporters and community managers, 'we identified the 252 most active Facebook pages and groups during the presidential campaign' (official party pages and groups, about 50 per political community). The 13.94% unreliable share is not in the abstract, which says only 'a clear over-representation of sources that are unreliable'. FLAG: the frozen row's denominator field is EMPTY.

abstract_quote: The aim of this study is to analyse the characteristics of the most shared news stories referencing the disease that circulated on SNSs, including the credibility of this content. ... We performed statistical and content analysis of the stories that had at least 1,000 total shares. ... The abundance of news stories in our sample (n = 1,594) were not classified according to their credibility
note: 'Most shared' is in the title and the Aim, and the >=1,000-share floor is in the abstract Methods. The abstract does not name Buzzsumo (Methods). The 13.05% rumour share is not in the abstract, which reports only that rumours 'are 3.29 times more shared than those considered scientifically correct'.

abstract_quote: In this cross-sectional study, the most viewed 60 videos were evaluated for global quality (GQS score), reliability (modified DISCERN score), usefulness (content-specific score), and misleading claims. ... Out of all videos, the speaker was a physician in 32% and misleading information was found in 42%.
note: 'Most viewed 60' is in the abstract. Methods: the first 100 most-viewed videos for the Arabic keyword, 60 retained. The Conclusion then generalises: 'YouTube is poorly informational on breast cancer and may be inaccurate in the Arab world where highly used.' The archived text is the Research Square preprint, not the Supportive Care in Cancer version of record.

abstract_quote: We examined 62 still-images and 64 video Instagram posts using #prostatecancer on 5/18/20. ... Of the 30% of content including objective information, 40% contained significant misinformation.
note: The abstract gives the hashtag, the date and n, but not the engagement ranking. Methods: 'We examined 150 posts (75 still-image posts with the most likes and 75 video posts with the most views listed as "hot")'. The Conclusion generalises: 'Instagram is a source of understandable PCa content ... had some misinformation.' The 40% rests on about 38 posts, a count the paper never prints.

abstract_quote: The criteria to select the videos on YouTube were the keywords “real food”, “realfood”, and “cancer” and the hashtags #realfood and #cancer were present, videos in English and videos available on 1 December 2022. ... Videos suggesting that the use of foods defined as “real food” could cure cancer without the intervention of any other treatment accounted for 12.5%.
note: The abstract presents the keyword/hashtag criteria as the whole selection rule and gives no n. Methods: of 3,817 videos retrieved, 'the ViewRatio of the resulting videos was calculated and the first 100 clips were selected', and 72 were retained after viewing. Coded not_stated because there is neither a rank cut nor a sample size (cf. 2-s2.0-86000670842). Borderline with sample_size_only, since the keyword frame is named.

abstract_quote: We instead present an analysis of data visualizations found in a real-world discourse of a significant global event—Twitter posts with visualizations related to the COVID-19 pandemic.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the 9,958 coded tweets come from random samples of COVID-19 tweets with images, filtered by text and image classifiers (Fig. 2 pipeline: 'Random sample of original English language tweets that contained images' ... 'Random sample taken from model' predictions). The 517 is a content-coded subset (opinion tweets supporting measures), with no rank cut or hand selection. The abstract gives no n and no percentage.

abstract_quote: This research note explores the extent to which misinformation and other types of “junk” content are spread on political boards and forums on 4chan and Reddit.
note: HKS Misinformation Review research note; the lead summary paragraph is the abstract. It gives no n and never says that only hostnames above a mention threshold were coded. Methods: 'we only coded websites with more than 2,000 mentions on Reddit and 400 on 4chan. This yielded 203 results from Reddit and 182 from 4chan.' This is the same frequency-truncation pattern as 2-s2.0-105021733739 in the September set. The 22% 'propaganda' figure is not in the abstract.

abstract_quote: This content analysis of six different national network transcripts highlights differences in coverage of severity, and the prevalence of misinformation and its correction that are consistent with previously established preferred news channels of conservatives/Republicans and liberals/Democrats
note: NOT_CURATED?: the 939 transcripts are a RANDOM 20% sample of each week's COVID-19 transcripts from six fixed national networks (Methods: 'A random integer set generator (random.org) was used to select a 20% sample of each week's transcripts to be coded'). The only hand choice is the six networks. The abstract gives no n and no percentage.

abstract_quote: Six different research terms were created for a search on YouTube. ... Of the videos evaluated, 78% were classified as useful, while the remaining 22% were misleading.
note: The abstract names a keyword search but gives no n and does not say that the 360 videos were taken from the first three pages of view-count-sorted results for each term (Methods; 142-144 analysed). This is the same pattern as 2-s2.0-85151113840 (neither a rank cut nor a sample size). A Romanian abstract carries the same text. The Conclusion generalises about misleading videos without the qualifier.

abstract_quote: Between April 16 and May 22, 2023, 37 different ophthalmology-relevant hashtags were queried on TikTok, and the top 20 most-liked videos per hashtag were analyzed. ... Misinformation was found in 5.4% of all videos, comprising 4.8% of all likes, 4.7% of all comments, and 11.7% of all bookmarks.
note: Clean disclosure: 'top 20 most-liked' per hashtag is in the abstract Methods, and the engagement-weighted 4.8% (the frozen curated row) is itself in the abstract. The Conclusion keeps the qualifier ('A significant portion of popular ophthalmologic content on TikTok').

abstract_quote: We searched TikTok on January 29, 2023, for sinusitis-related hashtags: #sinusitis, #sinus, #sinusinfection. ... There were 221 videos identified, which garnered over 300 million views and 1 million shares. ... Less than half of videos posted by nonmedical influencers categorized as educational were factual (46.7%); lay individuals and medical professionals had higher rates of factual educational content (79.9% and 83.7%, respectively).
note: The title says 'Popular Sinusitis Videos', which hints at a rule without naming it (cf. 2-s2.0-85085263461). Methods: 'One independent researcher collected the first 155 videos recommended by TikTok's standard search algorithm for each hashtag' (465 in total, 220 included). The abstract headlines factual rates by uploader on the curated educational subset, not the pooled 36% nonfactual. The Conclusion generalises: 'Most nonmedical influencer-posted TikTok videos about sinusitis are inaccurate'. The abstract says 221 videos; the body and frozen row say 220.

abstract_quote: we introduce a framework combining lab experiments (total N = 18,725), crowdsourcing, and machine learning to estimate the causal effect of 13,206 vaccine-related URLs on the vaccination intentions of US Facebook users ( N ≈ 233 million). ... Although misinformation reduced predicted vaccination intentions significantly more than unflagged vaccine content when viewed, Facebook users’ exposure to flagged content was limited.
note: Text: the abstract only (data/extract/include635_with_abstracts.jsonl); the full text is not in the local archive, so selection_in_methods is coded from the frozen rows and the 2026-11 extraction record (URLs shared publicly >100 times, published Q1 2021). The abstract gives n=13,206 but not the >100-share floor, which is the URL Shares dataset's privacy threshold rather than an author-chosen rank cut. The 0.3%, 5.1% and 1.4% shares are not in the abstract ('exposure to flagged content was limited'; '46-fold').

abstract_quote: Through a detailed examination of news-sharing sources, we uncover the widespread use of other media platforms like Telegram and YouTube for disseminating low-credibility information, indicating a concerning trend of diminishing news credibility over time.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the Telegram denominator is all messages of every public channel linked from the keyword-collected VaccinEU tweets (492 channels: 62 FR, 324 DE, 106 IT; Section on Telegram: 'Telegram links ... allowed us to get the information and content shared by different public channels'). There is no rank cut and no hand selection. The abstract gives no n and no percentage.

abstract_quote: Of the first 200 results under the search term “sarcoidosis,” all English-language videos with content directed at patients were included. ... Misinformation contained in the videos was described qualitatively. ... The majority of the 85 included videos were from an academic or governmental source (n = 63, 74%)
note: Clean first-200 disclosure in the abstract Methods. The 9% with incorrect or misleading facts is not in the abstract, where misinformation is 'described qualitatively'. The text is from data/fulltext/txt/ (no v2txt file).

abstract_quote: Results were sorted by relevance and the top 50 English-language results for each search were recorded. ... A total of 88 unique videos resulted from the search. ... None of the videos featured misleading information.
note: Clean top-50-by-relevance disclosure. The 0% is headlined as a count ('None of the videos'), coded yes as for 2-s2.0-85129456715.

abstract_quote: We used the term “epilepsy” on the native search function of TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts to construct a videobase of 250 videos per platform. ... In total, 102 videos (18.1% [14.9–21.3]) were classified as containing disinformation/misinformation; TikTok has the highest proportion (31.7% [24.7%- 38.8]).
note: Names the search and the 250-per-platform cap but not the word 'first' (coded stated, as for 2-s2.0-105004460836); Methods: 'A total of 750 video URLs were recorded, 250 from each social media platform', blank account, relevance-ordered results. The Significance section generalises: 'Disinformation/misinformation regarding epilepsy is seen in almost a fifth of videos on short-form content platforms'. The abstract says 563 retained; the frozen pooled row says 562.

abstract_quote: In this data memo we apply a tested dictionary of sources about political news and information being shared over Twitter over a ten day period around the 2016 Presidential Election. ... We find that (1) nationally, Twitter users got more misinformation, polarizing and conspiratorial content than professionally produced news.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the denominator is all links in hashtag-collected election tweets from US-located users (Methods: 'Tweets were selected based on a list of hashtags'), a topical keyword sample (cf. the September flag on 2-s2.0-85074511992). The abstract gives no n, no hashtag rule and no percentage, but makes a national comparative prevalence claim.

abstract_quote: Ten search terms were employed to search for and analyze 200 videos about climate and climate modification topics, which are contested topics in online media. The online anonymization tool Tor has been used for the randomization of the sample and to avoid personalization of the results. ... 16 videos deny anthropogenic climate change and 91 videos in the sample propagate straightforward conspiracy theories about climate engineering and climate change.
note: The abstract gives n=200 and the number of terms, but not that the sample is the first 20 results per term (Methods: 'the first 20 videos', 'The first 20 results encompass ... its first result page'). 'Randomization of the sample' can be misread as random sampling, although Tor was only used to depersonalise results. The 8% is headlined as a count (16 of 200).

abstract_quote: To that end, 1000 tweets have been analyzed. Results show that false information is tweeted more but retweeted less than science-based evidence or fact-checking tweets
note: The abstract gives n=1000 only. Methods, Criterion 5: 'the 1000 tweets with more RT have been selected'. The abstract's prevalence claim ('false information is tweeted more') rests on the top-1000-retweeted set without saying so. No percentage in the abstract.

abstract_quote: We compile a list of 1,073 news websites and extract posts from four Web communities (Twitter, Reddit, 4chan, and Gab) that contain URLs from these sources. This yields a dataset of 38M posts containing 15M news URLs, spanning almost three years.
note: The abstract names the domain-list selection but not how the list was built. Methods: the top 30K Majestic domains, filtered to the VirusTotal news category and to NewsGuard-rated sites, giving 1,073. The denominator is ALL posts linking to these sites, so the curation is at domain level (a popularity-ranked list), not item level. Borderline: the author may treat it as not curated (cf. the September flag on 2-s2.0-85091698994). No percentage in the abstract ('disproportionately referencing untrustworthy sources').

abstract_quote: One-hundred trending videos were identified from the hashtag #covidvaccine and were coded for content. Collectively, these videos garnered over 35 million views. ... Twenty-two of these 38 videos (57.89%) falsely conveyed that a vaccine was available, as they were not at the time of the study.
note: Clean 'trending' disclosure. The frozen curated row (43% of cumulative views to false-availability videos) is not in the abstract, which headlines view shares by encourage/discourage category and the 22-of-38 false-availability figure within the discouraging subset.

abstract_quote: In this study, we analyze for the first time newly available engagement data covering millions of web links shared on Facebook to describe how and by which categories of U.S. users different types of news are seen and shared on the platform. ... Across the platform, however, articles from credible news sources are shared over 5 times more often and viewed over 7 times more often than articles from low-credibility sources.
note: The abstract never says the links are only those shared publicly at least 100 times (Methods: 'we only have access to news links shared at least 100 times publicly'; the Condor URL dataset privacy floor), yet it says 'Across the platform'. 'Millions of web links' gives only an order of magnitude. The headline is a ratio (5x shares, 7x views), not a percentage, so headline is coded no.

abstract_quote: In this work, we compare the dissemination of misinformation on Twitter about the approval of such a vaccine for adults and children. The results show that misinformation is significant on Twitter and there has been a substantial change in the style of such content shared between 2021 and 2022
note: The abstract gives no n and no rule. Methods: 'we manually labeled the tweets with at least one retweet' (quotes counted as retweets), giving 1,010 (2021) and 816 (2022) 'coronavac' tweets from the two approval days. The selection is an engagement floor (>=1 retweet) on a one-day keyword collection, weaker than a rank cut; the author may consider it not curated. The abstract generalises: 'misinformation is significant on Twitter'.

abstract_quote: The first 120 videos found which met the inclusion criteria (English speaking, duration greater than one minute, greater than 500 views, renal cancer addressed) were selected. ... the grading for overall level of misinformation was moderate.
note: Clean first-120 disclosure, with the >500-view floor. There is no misinformation percentage in the abstract; the 49.2% and 22.5% derive from the Table 4 score counts. The Conclusion generalises: 'The quality of information accessed from YouTube on kidney cancer is of a low to moderate overall standard with significant levels of misinformation.'

abstract_quote: Mediante técnicas computacionales de monitoreo, recolección y procesamiento de datos extraídos de la plataforma, se compuso una muestra de los 100 mensajes más compartidos de cada uno de los conflictos (n=300). [Article's own English abstract: 'Through monitoring computational techniques, gathering and processing extracted data from the platform, a sample of the 100 most shared messages of each conflict (n=300) was composed.']
note: Clean top-100-per-conflict disclosure in both the Spanish and the English abstract. The 31.7% is not in the abstract, which says 'a large amount of content with information disorders among the most shared posts'.

abstract_quote: We recruited 99 users who installed a browser extension that enabled us to collect up-next recommendation trails and search results for 45 videos and 88 search queries about the 2020 elections. We find that YouTube’s search results, irrespective of search query bias, contain more videos that oppose rather than support election misinformation.
note: The abstract gives the 88 queries and 99 users, but not that the queries were researcher-curated or that only the top ten standard search results per query were analysed (Methods: 'we consider the top ten search results'). There is no percentage, only the comparative 'more videos that oppose rather than support'.

abstract_quote: Data was collected from the top-performing 600 posts on Instagram, under the top six key search words related to diabetes and its management. ... Only 448 out of 600 posts were found to be relevant to the study. ... The authenticity of the information was not determined in 221 posts (49.33%) whereas misinformation was seen in 19 posts (4.24%).
note: Clean 'top-performing' disclosure (top 100 per hashtag x 6). The 4.24% denominator includes the 221 posts whose authenticity was undetermined.

abstract_quote: Leveraging an updated version of the same data source — Meta’s URL Shares Dataset — and replicating much of the methodology, we quantify the trustworthy and untrustworthy links to external websites that have been shared on Facebook in the period between 2019 and 2022 in three major European countries (Germany, France, and Italy). We observe a clear decline in the number of URLs present in the dataset and an increase in the URLs from untrustworthy domains as a percentage of the total URLs shared in a year.
note: The abstract names the dataset but not its 100-public-share floor (Methods: 'the threshold of 100 public shares'), and gives no n and no percentage. Coded not_stated (dataset named, selection rule and size absent). The same Condor floor applies to W3161533314.

abstract_quote: (no abstract - Skin Research and Technology research letter; opening methods text: "To carry out our study, we first searched TikTok using “#Psoriasis” and navigated our way to the hashtag section. From here, we selected the first 200 videos to include in our study.")
note: Research letter with no abstract. The body states the first-200 rule and the 45% (21 of 47 educational videos deemed unreliable).

abstract_quote: To answer these questions, we analyzed 13 million messages from 1,444 political groups over seven months from July 2022 to January 2023. Using network analysis, our findings suggest a significant prevalence of coordinated activity in the propagation of news messages, 26% of which originate from misinformation sites.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the 26% denominator is the links in messages posted near-simultaneously by >=2 coordinated accounts, a behaviour-defined (algorithmic) subset of all messages in 1,444 public political groups, with no rank cut or hand pick. The abstract names the coordinated-activity scope, but '26% of which' is ambiguous between news messages and links.

abstract_quote: The first 200 videos retrieved using the keywords “boca ferida radioterapia” [“sore mouth radiotherapy”] were analyzed, excluding those shorter than 1 min, longer than 15 min, or unrelated to the topic. ... Of the 104 videos analyzed, 51.0% were produced by doctors and 85.6% were aimed at the lay public. ... Overall, 10.6% (n = 11) were classified as ‘poor’ due to the presence of misinformation.
note: Clean first-200 disclosure. The closing sentence keeps the national scope ('few videos on radiotherapy-related OM in Brazil presented incorrect information').

abstract_quote: The dataset used in this study consists of 5,385 comments collected from TikTok and Facebook through web scraping techniques.
note: NOT_CURATED?: Methods say only that 5,385 comments 'related to discussions about the Prabowo-era government were collected' via Apify. No rank cut, keyword list, post or account selection is documented, so the curated label rests on an undocumented topical scrape. The 23% hoax share appears only in the Methods data description, not in the abstract (which reports classifier accuracies).

abstract_quote: Within the scope of the research, 150 pieces of content selected through purposive sampling from seven different digital platforms were evaluated using FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) spectrum analysis and qualitative content analysis techniques. The findings of the technical analysis reveal that a remarkably high proportion of the examined content, 92%, did not contain the specific frequency values promised in their titles
note: 'Purposive sampling' is named, but the abstract omits the criteria (Methods: 'at least 10,000 interactions and included a specific Hz value in its title or description'). Because every item was selected for making a Hz claim, the 92% is conditional on the claim.

abstract_quote: YouTube and TikTok were searched using the hashtags #alopecia and #alopeciatreatment. Posts were selected based on hashtag relevance. ... Among videos specifically discussing AA treatment, 56% of YouTube videos and 73%of TikTok videos were categorized as “accurate and medical data–backed.”
note: NOT_CURATED?: the curated rows' denominators (23 YouTube and 52 TikTok treatment videos) are a topical subset of hashtag-retrieved videos; Methods give no rank cut or cap, only hashtag relevance and exclusions. The abstract names the treatment subset and headlines its accuracy shares (56%/73%). The subset's misinformation and limited-evidence shares (0%/3%, 43%/23%) are in the body only; the whole-sample misinformation shares (0%/1%) are headlined.

abstract_quote: Using two datasets totaling roughly 14 billion search engine result pages (SERPs) from Bing, the second most popular search engine in the U.S., we show that search exposes users to few unreliable information sources.
note: NOT_CURATED?: both samples are random (a simple random sample of search results and a weighted random sample of >100,000 information-seeking queries; Introduction and Fig. 1 legends). The 'top 3' rows are rank positions within a results page (the exposure unit), not a sample truncation. No percentage in the abstract.

abstract_quote: Employing a novel data donation model, we developed a tool that allows users to voluntarily share their interactions with public Facebook groups and pages, which we subsequently enrich using CrowdTangle. This approach enabled the collection and analysis of a dataset comprising over 1,200 American users.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the denominator is all URLs in the 16 million posts of the pages and groups followed by 1,261 data-donating users, a participant-defined census of followed sources with no rank cut. The abstract names the donation mechanism. The 0.01% low-quality share is not in the abstract; its 17% is political content.

abstract_quote: Analyzing a large-scale dataset from Twitter/X related to the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election, we find that approximately 12% of shared images are detected as AI-generated, and around 10% of users are responsible for sharing 80% of AI-generated images.
note: NOT_CURATED?: the dataset is a keyword-query collection ('querying targeted keywords related to political figures, events, and emerging issues'; 2.5M images, Jul-Sep 2024), a full topical sample with no rank cut. The abstract gives the topic but neither n nor the keyword rule. The 12% is AI-generated images, which are not misinformation per se.
